newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Railtrack year profits gather steam.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Railtrack year profits gather steam.

text.p: British railways operator Railtrack Plc will move back into the political spotlight next Thursday when it announces a near 60 percent rise in profits in its first year's results since privatisation.
Analysts expect the company to report underlying pre-tax profits of around 300 million stg for the year to March 31, from 190 million stg last time.
The final dividend is expected to be raised to 14.7 pence a share from 13.75p last time, making 22p for the year on earnings up 10 pence at around 53 pence.

But the pre-tax result will be flattered by a sharp drop in interest charges, thanks to the hefty debt write-off it enjoyed before being sold off last May. Investors who bought the company for 1.93 billion stg are already enjoying an embarassment of riches, seeing the share price rise from the equivalent of 3.80 stg partly-paid, at flotation, to 640-1/2p on Friday.

For the current year this puts the share on a rating of just over 11 times forecast earnings and promises a gross yield of 4.6 percent at current tax rates, according to market forecasts provided on Reuters by Edinburgh Financial Publishing.
But Railtrack is now in the line of fire for the new Labour government's proposed windfall tax on excessive profits made by privatised utilities.

And it remains to be seen whether the company can prove to the government that it can indeed create as promised, "the best railway in the world," when Labour in opposition had called the privatisation "an act of vandalism".
"We don't like the share because of the political risk," said one broker on Friday.
But another said: "It's a solid hold with good long-term profits growth from a strong asset base which has considerable scope for improved asset utilisation."
Labour has threatened a tougher regulatory regime for Railtrack, following sharp criticisms by the industry regulator Ofrail that the company was lagging behind in its spending promises.

Railtrack last year promised to spend 15.9 billion stg on maintenance and renovation of the network over the next decade and has said the delays were justified by preparatory work being done on where to spend the money.
Earlier this month chairman Sir Robert Horton launched what he called the start of a "rail renaissance" with plans to spend one billion stg on upgrading 2,500 stations across Britain.
He also denied that liability to the windfall tax would have any influence on spending plans.
"We have provided for this expenditure in our balance sheet and we have made a promise on this. We will spend this money," he said.
